p:
So, complaints in general go through 311, and 311 has access to Language Line for any of hundred+ languages, right? Complaints about harassment might come to our Anti-harassment Unit. We also as an agency, and I would hazard [sic] to guess that most agencies do have Language Line as an option, right? So, whoever calls in whatever language, the option is to get Language Line on the phone. When we’re dealing through our Partners in Preservation, often they have staff who speak those languages and can do kind of that translation for us. So, I think there’s

a number of options. These are the types of materials I think– this one’s in English, obviously, but that was designed with the joint agencies and delivered through our Partners in Preservation, organizers, our community-based organization partners, or through our staff to tenants so that they know how to navigate the system in terms of the harassment specifically. Because sometimes the harassment isn’t related directly to the conditions. The landlord may just want the tenants to leave.
Yeah. I mean, sometimes they want them to raise the rent to a ridiculous amount as well. Like, there’s a [inaudible].
Right.

Okay. And then so, what– can you walk me through so that process when they call, what kind of information is required from the tenant to give you? What kind of personal information do they– do you require for it?
When filing a complaint with HPD–
[interposing] Yes.
we require– in most cases, if the condition is in your apartment, we need your name and we need your apartment and your building address. That is all.
Okay.

And whatever condition you’re complaining about. For conditions like heat and hot water, you can report that anonymously. So we would encourage folks, and this is the very reason, even going back many, many years why we allow anonymous complaints to be made. Not just immigration harassment, but harassment of any kind.
And so going back to CONH, does HPD currently have the capacity to proactive investigate buildings on the pilot list that show indicators of repeated complaints or vacancies?

So, HPD has other programs that work proactively. The CONH program is an after-the-fact program. When an owner

applies for Department of Buildings permit. HPD also has an Anti-harassment Unit that does things proactively. So we run a slightly different list of buildings, but it is also a building– I’m sorry, a list that has buildings with many of the same characteristics, high violations of hours, complaints at DOB, potentially other agencies, and we proactively send inspectors to those buildings. We don’t wait for a complaint to come in.
So, do they ever overlap in that way? Like, does it ever get–

[interposing] A lot of our programs overlap. So, you can select a– just because a building is on the CONH pilot list does not mean that it will not be identified through the Anti-harassment Unit and proactive inspections conducted.
Okay. Last one. Do you know how many of the buildings on the pilot list receive any form of city subsidy, tax exemption, public financing?

Thank you very much for that question. I don’t believe we

usually track that. We did that question, so we are looking into that data, and we’re happy to share that once we put that together.
Yeah. I have other– you know, I wasn’t– we’re still trying to figure out how we were doing all the questioning, so I was focusing most of my questions– I have questions for you, don’t worry.
Okay.
But I’m also going to try to open it up to some of the other Council Members here so that they can ask their questions, but I’ll leave that to the Chair to manage.
Thank you, Chair. So, now we’ll turn to Council Member colleague questions. First up is Council Member Zhuang.

Thank you, Chair, and also I want to thank everyone come here for testify. I have a question. When we talk about tenants and the landlord call them ICE– I have a situation in my district. A developer calling, harassing people in the neighborhood saying if you

keep protesting here, we’re going to call police. You’re going to get arrested. We’ll call ICE on you. You’re going to get deported. This type of situation, which department I can go to make a complaint? Is HPD, MOIA, or– it’s a developer.

Yeah, I would say that all– just to start, all New Yorkers regardless of immigration status or national origin have the same housing rights. In that case, we would encourage folks to call the New York City Commission on Human Rights, developer or not, to file a complaint. But I don’t know if you want to add anything else.
Yeah, if you–
[interposing] It’s the developer. It’s not renter and landlord.

If you believe that the developer is one that works with HPD, you can certainly reach out to us. I’m not familiar with the developers in my day-to-day work, but we’re happy to take your complaint and look into it for whatever we can identify.
Thank you. And also, from the program, are tenants aware of this program? And what’s the language where you guys doing outreach? How many language do you have?
Thank you. You’re talking specifically about the Certificate of No Harassment program?
Yes.
Or you’re talking about–
No Harassment program.

So, when a building applies for the program, we do notice the building and we do send investigators out. We will make sure that the information that we give out is in, and the– I think– believe the bill lists out the– it should be the 10 languages, right, which we put most of our materials in. so, we will make sure that that is encompassed there, and we appreciate that change.

Because most of the people get harassed are immigrants and they– a

lot of them don’t speak English at all. So, if the team doing reaching out in English, it’s very hard for people to know. In my district, a lot of people have no idea about this program.

Thank you, Council Member. We’re definitely going to work make sure that as much as we can in the 10 language that everything is understandable and that they have someone to reach to. Again, if someone should see our notice and call the Certificate of No Harassment program, they have access to Language Line to be able to talk back and forth and translate that information.

Appreciate it. Thank you. And also, I have the situation in my district, because ICE came to the neighborhood, a lot of people living in that neighborhood just ran away, the people that don’t have document. Any way HPD can help those people?
I would turn that question to MOIA. I know they do a lot of outreach in neighborhoods just in general on immigrant rights. So, let me–

Yeah, we’re happy to follow up on that. And even thinking about your first question, because I think your first question I might have answered it wrong. We can follow up too with the development question, because I think that’s a little bit different, and I know that was mentioned than a landlord. And then in regards to outreach, I don’t know how often we have been in your neighborhood, but I can get back to you. I’m happy to–
[interposing] We have a situation. ICE came in, take one person away. I actually know the people leaving the building. They just moved. They’re scared to live there any more.
Okay, got it.
Like every single one don’t have document in that area. Everyone moved.
Because they’re afraid that–
[interposing] Yes. Thank you.
Okay. Thank you, Council Member Zhuang. Council Member Joseph followed by Council Member Maloney then Avilés.

Thank you. Good morning. Couple of questions. You said a couple of great things, right? So, the off– to file the harassment complaint, the Certificate of No Harassment, how long does it take, and what are the criteria for the buildings to get on? And if they do want to apply, language access and language barriers usually the one– the main things that our communities of immigrants face. Can you walk us through the process?

Certainly. Thank you. So, the Certificate of No Harassment program as we’re explaining is a program of deterrence, right? The idea is that identifying buildings that have certain characteristics, and just in general, those characteristics include violations, emergency repair charges, the building is an early alternative enforcement program, right, or the 7A program, there’s been a vacate order, although not a fire vacate, right? [inaudible] and a harassment

finding, right? So, if there’s been a finding of harassment against the property already in a court, those buildings are included. I am not the data person. So, if you really want to drill down, I can bring Assistant Commissioner back up, but the idea is that those characteristics are weighed against other similar buildings at the time that the list run. Right? The buildings get on the list. The owners are notified that they are on the list, and that if they wish to do certain work which is referred to as covered categories of work. When they apply for those– when they put those applications and apply for those permits from the Department of Buildings, they must get the sign-off from the HPD that after an investigation, we found no evidence of harassment in the five years prior to tehir application.

So, I have a building in my district, 75 Lennox [sp?] Road who’s been on the news, that’s– the management made sure that folks were walking around with security hats to intimidate the tenants, knocking on their doors. Then, within two days, ICE showed up at the building. So, this was a form of harassment, but I’m sure the

tenants in those buildings don’t know about this program that you talk about, because that building has several violations, many violations. And we did a walk-through. We met with the tenant association, and then we met with another building that said the minute they call 311, management is already at their door saying why are you calling 311?
And I’d be– I don’t know this building as on the list or not, Council Member, but we’d be happy to talk with you further about this.
I would love that.
If the building is on the list, talk to you about what next steps we can–
[interposing] Yeah, I would love to do that along with their tenant association. When HPD go on site and they find let’s say an ICE agent, what is the protocol?

Again, as I mentioned to the Chair, we have not yet had that to my knowledge to have that happen. But in any case

where an inspector goes on site or a field staff person really, because we do have other field staff that go to buildings as well, the protocol is to escalate that within the agency. So, certainly, I would know if that has happened. We would take appropriate steps depending on the facts of what is actually happening the building at that case. So, I think, you know, our inspectors are fairly good at identifying unusual situations such as I would imagine that would be.
At 75 Lennox Road.
I’m talking about if they come across–
[interposing] Were to encounter–
Yes.

ICE. And MOIA, what are in place for you to work with HPD, DOB, if these situation occurs? What resources are out there, or community engagement for communities to know that these programs exist? Sometime we do great work, but no one knows it exists.

Yeah, thank you for that– we’ve developed– well, there’s several just guidance that we have that include our MOIA one-pager, and that includes also information for New Yorkers. It’s available in over 50 languages, tenant rights. We’ve collaborated with CCHR to put together immigrants and New York City Human Rights working at housing. HPD also mentioned this other flyer that we put together with immigrants Know Your Rights in housing PEU. We also supported them in putting together a KYR that they have available at the portal of information and rights that they have regardless of status, and as well as the Tenant Bill of Rights.
Are these information also located inside of Housing Court?
I don’t have the answer.
I think that would be a great place to start as well.
I would also say, and I– listing all those documents reminded me. When our inspectors do any inspection, we give out a pamphlet about–
[interposing] Okay.
a host of housing issues.
Right.

I think one of them on there is harassment. It’s not currently specific to immigration harassment, but it gives them a referral to CCHR and it provides them information on contacts on who they can go to if they feel they’re being harassed. The definition of what harassment is, that pamphlet is available in 10 languages. We have a QR code on the back for people to scan and it says in the 10 languages if you want a copy of this in Spanish, scan the QR code and takes them to our website where they can find that document in their language.

In a time– in the moment that we are in right now, I hope there’s a lot of collaboration into agency to make this work seamless as our tenants in New York City face a high rate of harassment, and folks are banking on this idea of ICE being in buildings to make sure they’re

scarring tenants. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chairs.

Yeah. Thank you very much, Council Member. And under EO13, as I mentioned, the agencies are in a very coordinated way working towards making this information very educational and directed to the folks who need it.

Great. Thank you so much, Council Member. And the question that you raised about the property in your district, I think that’s a big part of the reason why we do want a faster refresh of the data so that we can be capturing buildings in more than a five-year cadence. It’s really great feedback. Thank you. Council Member Avilés? COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. Good afternoon. Thank you for being here. I wanted to– the issue that many immigrant communities face is an issue of overcrowding in units and all the safety that– safety issues that emerge from those kinds of conditions. Is HPD giving any incoming around like

severe overcrowding, and how are you addressing that issue?

Thank you, Council Member. So, our inspectors have dealt with overcrowding over the years. I don’t think it’s a new issue for us. To the extent that we can allow people to remain in place, we do. I can’t think of a recent incident where we found such significant overcrowding that a vacate was necessary on a large scale. We have in the past found those things. I think our goal is to make sure that people are safe. Right? To the extent possible. As you know, or as some of you may know, when we issue a vacate order, people do have our emergency housing process available to them, and that is also regardless of immigration status. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And in terms of– thank you. I mean, I think, obviously, it is an issue that has persisted over decades and obviously with the cost of rent in this city, it is no surprise that both in immigrant communities and non-immigrant communities you’d have overcrowding in units just to try to pay for them. However, there have been a number of issues related to overcrowding that we’ve

got to figure out how to address, particularly in immigrant communities who have language isolation and maybe do not understand or have not had access to the kinds of programs information that the city has at its disposal. In terms of the Certificate of No Harassment process, once the average time from application to determination?

For the pilot period it was even months. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: And is– what– seems like a long time. A lot happens in seven months. What kinds of elements determine that timeframe, and has HPD looked at ways to reduce that timeframe?

So, there are set periods in the law for us to do outreach. There’s a 45-day response period that we can extend to 60 days. Our teams need to go out and speak to the residents, right, and we try to find people who used to live there as part of the application. It's not only the owner giving us information about the people who are currently living at the building, but any information they might have about people who have

moved during the period, where they have contact information. So, it does take us some time generally to do all of that investigation and outreach. That average also includes cases where there were initial determinations of harassment which maybe take a little bit longer time, because we really need to prepare after there’s that initial determination of harassment. There’s an OATH hearing, right, that needs to occur before the certificate is denied. We continue to look as always at administratively how you can reduce the time. We did have, as mentioned before, early in the period, right, coming out of COVID. You know, we had some staffing challenges, and now we’re in a better place. And I think we will continue to try and for those landlords who have not harassed, right– we make a determination that there was no harassment, and we grant that certificate to try and minimize the time for that process. But again, we want to make sure that we’re thorough, that we’ve investigated all potential allegations of harassment. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you. In terms of any specific data, have you noted data–

obviously you’re not 311. But have you noted any data at the intersection of, you know, immigration enforcement, harassment that I think would– I guess do you have any data on that at all.

I don’t at HPD. I think that might be a focus of this EO13 group, you know, to start looking at data across various challenges that immigrants are facing. I don’t know. I’ll turn it to my colleagues at MOIA if they have any data.
We don’t have anything regarding 311, but we do have data regarding the Ask MOIA hotline where folks call–

Thank you for that question, Chairs. So, in 2025, there were 151 calls to the MOIA hotline or emails to the email account having to do with housing, and that covers a wide swath of things. It’s case of harassment. That’s cases of folks looking for what types of housing assistance they may be eligible for. We don’t break it down any further than that beyond it being housing related, but we do understand that that is a need.

COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: What was the percentage of the total related to housing?

It’s about a little bit under 10 percent of the total calls that have come in and emails that have come in are related to housing. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Okay. It would be great to understand disaggregated– that disaggregated data given it is a small subset. It would be helpful to know what the buckets are that are concerning community members who are engaged in making that outreach. We want to make sure we’re able to respond to them.

Thank you, Council Member Avilés. Just a quick follow-up on the investigation that HPD conducts. So, you are not looking for harassment yourself as an agency. You’re looking to external decisions on whether harassment has been found, is that right? And then what are you looking for?

Yeah. We– and to answer this question more fully, I’m going to

call up Assistant Commissioner Weithman who oversees the program to give a more thorough answer.
Thank you.

Thank you for that question. So, the investigation includes– our investigators speak with former and current tenants. They do research in all of the city databases to find any violations, obviously issued by HPD, but also from DOB, the Health Department. It’s a very broad-reaching investigation. We also look at HCR data. We visit the building. We do inspections, and based on the investigator’s report, it then goes through a legal review. And so that’s based on all the interviews of current and former tenants, as well as any stakeholders in the communities. We do get often– sometimes we get comments from elected officials office, obviously from CBOs and legal services providers. So, it’s not so much of looking– if HCR has issued a determination of harassment, we would have known that, but it’s really about our assessment of all of the data that we are collecting to make our own assessment as to whether or not we

believe there’s reasonable cause that harassment did occur.
Got it. Thank you so much. That’s really helpful. So, now back to Chair Encarnacion.

Thank you. I am– you know, a lot of the questions about the timing and stuff is really important because I guess now with the harassment, it’s like that threat is a phone call away from tearing someone’s life away, apart. You know, and so it is the urgency of following up on these calls is really important, and I’m you know, hearing that 10 percent of the calls to MOIA kind of fall under that cross-section. It’s surprising quite frankly. So I wanted to kind of understand how do you current define immigration status based tenant harassment?

I mean, the callers themselves would identify it. So, they would say– I can give you one example of a caller coming in and saying my landlord wants me out because– and people will say because I’m an immigrant. I would take that very broadly, and I know that the question

was raised before regarding some of the buckets which we don’t have handy, but that’s like a very broad sort of statement that we’ve received from our External Affairs arm who manages some of these phone calls.

So, the things like a whole building not having heat or hot water and then, you know, you seeing like further down the line, would that be tagged or flagged as possibly an immigrant-based threat or tactic or whatever by the landlord?
Yeah. so, I can walk you through what happens now.
Okay.

I think that might sort of help based on how the calls and what we’ve received them. Typically, we get calls connected to code violations. So, if there’s repairs– to the question you just asked, and if people say that it’s basis of like natural origin or harassment, we refer those to HPD. we go a little bit further there. If there’s additional questions that are identified as like this is something that’s

constant, we’ll also make a referral to CCHR, to the Commission on Human Rights so folks have the ability to file complaints against that landlord based on harassment issues like that.
Does anybody go out to the building?

Currently we don’t have people that go out into the building. However, we did do some work with overseeing just where the buildings are, the program that’s being talked about. Our outreach team has been in the neighborhoods since the beginning of the year. We’ve been in about 61 percent of the buildings that are part of the pilot program, and that was just in the beginning of January. We find that with immigrants especially the first touchpoint is also just to share information of what the thing might be called and identified as, and that’s part of some of the work that we’ve done in the outreach level, but we haven’t directly been deployed or go to buildings per say.

Yeah, I think that that’s where people are kind of falling through the cracks, because there’s calls being made of– that

all are kind of flagging possible tenant harassment due to this, but then nobody’s really follow– like, the onus is on the tenant to explicitly say and then look for resources and then connect to folks, and I think that– you know, if there was someone kind of going on and following up on these calls, which I know that, you know, one of the issues is MOIA’s current headcount and the budget that you have for tenant outreach. So, can you talk a little bit about that and how– what that looks like, what is the current headcount specifically for tenant outreach, Know Your Rights education, and– yeah.
So, MOIA doesn’t have currently a division dedicated to tenant outreach, but we do embed that work across our work as an agency, especially in our outreach team which consists of 17 individuals.
How?
What type of work they do you mean?
Yeah, like how is that embedded in–

[interposing] And then I could also just talk about MOIA just overall. So, with the External Affairs team, as I mentioned as one of the data points, we have folks who are deployed to immigrant dense neighborhoods. Again, 61 percent of them have been deployed to the districts or zip codes in which the pilot program that we're talking about at the beginning of the year have been providing, again, information regarding tenant rights generally. In connection to the work that we also do with our communications arm, we’ve also developed– and this was mentioned in the testimony, but we created and develop– support in developing a flyer and held a roundtable to share out information– this was back in 2025– on some of the issues that we were hearing regarding tenant harassment. So, those are two sort of touch points that are both with our external and outreach arm as well as with our communications arm.

Yeah. I’m always going to, you know, fight for more to be done there. I just think that it’s really hard, and that’s one of the hardest things about, you know, tenant

organizing is that you have to kind of go out to the– and build that trust with the residents and be on site with the tenants and connect them to those resources. It’s laborious work and it’s not easy, right? But it’s necessary if we’re going to start identifying and protecting tenants so they can feel safer, because right now the onus is really on them to step forward and that’s a really scary thing and a really scary reality right now. So, I’m trying to, you know, kind of get to that point. So, when you do have a connection with someone who is facing harassment for the basis of– for the basis of their immigration status, what guidance do you have for them? Like, what do you tell them to do?

Yeah, we certainly inform them of their right to connect with either 311 or the Commission on Human Rights. If they’re interested in filing a complaint as well as sharing that they could, you know, speak with– based on the language that they speak, that they can be filing those complaints. So, we do direct folks to CCHR.

But that’s– so you’re– they’re calling you and you’re telling them to call someone else. That’s what I’m trying to get to. So, there’s no connecting– MOIA connecting directly to those services. They would then just know that they could go and get the services elsewhere?

That’s what’s been done in the past, and I think Commissioner Ali [sic] when she first came to testify she indicated and mentioned that we as MOIA will be even more embedded within the affordability agenda. So step one of what we’ve done is increased the outreach to some of these neighborhoods that we’ve mentioned. Currently, the process is as I mentioned, but I know that after this hearing and also based again on the needs across the city and citywide efforts, connected to the affordability agenda with the mayor there will be potential other touch points, but that’s currently what we have as it stands.
Okay, perfect. And I will–

[interposing] And again, I’d like to say the Partners in Preservation program, through their community organizers, again, if you have not seen the flyer, we certainly can get those for you– are also in the neighborhoods, in the buildings talking to people and directing them directly to the Commission on Human Rights.

Awesome. Thank you. Yeah. I just feel like there’s a lot being surfaced that’s really helpful for us to know and understand and, you know, continue to push for and during the budget process as well. I have some more questions, but I kind of just– I feel compelled to make a statement, in part because of my constituents and some of the things– some of rhetoric that I hear on the ground sometimes, and then of course you know, it’s repeated in the media about how immigrants get everything. Immigrants are taking advantage of so many services, and the reality that– I think and our committee report has highlighted and what we’re talking about here today, that, you know, immigrant New Yorkers and particularly undocumented immigrant

New Yorkers are really not eligible for most of the programs that the city has available. And so when we’re talking about the anti-harassment programs that you all run and that we’re trying to strengthen here today through the Certificate of No Harassment, it’s just really critical work, because there are immigrant New Yorkers and particularly our undocumented immigrant New Yorkers are already living in such precarious conditions. So we really do have to advance this work further. So, I want to follow up on a question that I asked before, but from the DOB perspective. If our Assistant Commissioner could join us at the dais. Again, it’s a fun game of musical chairs. We’re going to administer the oath and then I’ll go into the question.

Please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions? Thank you. You may proceed.

Thank you, Assistant Commissioner. So, HPD touched on this earlier. HPD CONH pilot program report indicated

that when buildings are placed on the list they tend to avoid undertaking serious projects that would require certification. DOB foresee– sorry, that sentence is not very good looking English. Well, essentially the question is from DOB’s perspective. Do you– do you see any essential work being delayed from buildings that are participants in the CONH program that are on the list?

Well, the program is the deterrent, and I think that reflects in the numbers, and the essential work whether it’s gas or plumbing or electrical or essential services, that is something that is a carve-out and we do proceed with that, right? The CONH program is really there to prevent changes in the layout, right, and changes to the occupancy of the building or to see major changes that room count or the number of units. So, those essential services would not be held up unless they’re all combined together. They file one large application. So, those are things that could complicated it, but yeah, that’s where we come in when we see something like if a building is vacated. Right? That’s a situation

where exceptions are made, right? If there’s a fire or something along those lines or a structural issues.

Thank you. Have you– have we seen a lot of these sort of bigger applications that have alteration work, but also some of the essential work? I mean, and then just getting to the bottom of it, I think I just really want to make sure that from the agency’s perspective there is not the thinking that these buildings are putting off any essential work, any work that is essential to the health and safety of tenants?
That’s not what we generally see. That’s like a complicated type of situation. To try to answer your question, that’s how essential work might be delayed, but the architects and engineers–
[interposing] But it can be disaggregated.

The architects and engineers that file these jobs, they’re aware of the CONH limits. And if they put in extra work that will limit them from getting their

permit, it’ll complicate it. So they will specifically put in– they have to answer a question that says are you changing the layout? If they check no, they can proceed with their permit. If they check yes, then they have to the CONH, and then they then get restricted by the program. So, they are aware of the restrictions.

Yeah. No, that makes a lot of sense, and does HPD– have you’ve received applications for CONH like that where it’s a big scope of work? Do you advise them to separate the work so that the essential work is completed? Welcome back, Marti.

Thank you, Chair. From HPD’s perspective, we really rely on DOB to make– to identify the buildings that do require the CONH. so we don’t necessarily dig into the plans. So, I can’t really speak to how often that happens.

Okay. Does HPD or Buildings, do you have any recommendations or changes in the definition of covered work for this either because we want to make sure that no essential work

is, you know, not being done, or because there’s other categories of work that we should be limiting for covered buildings?
At this time, we do not have any recommendations to expand that definition.

Okay. Thank you. Okay, so moving back to just the structure of the program, local and state laws often change what constitutes tenant harassment. How does– two part question. How does the CONH integrate any changes from other local laws? And second, the first pilot was before the HSTPA that strengthened rent laws in New York City, and then the pilot extension was after HSTPA. So, I’m curious of HPD has analyzed or uncovered any changes in the landscape for CONH covered buildings in the pilot versus the pilot extension.

Thank you, Council Member. Definitely the change with the HG– with the state laws impacted the incentive to harass tenants how to be able to increase the rent, you tremendously upon vacancy. And so, we would have to

say that definitely those changes have made this type of harassment less profitable, right? I think that that’s clear. I think in terms of doing any specific analysis around it, I don’t think that we have done that. I will turn it over to Assistant Commissioner Srini.

It’s limited, but we do– we did look at rent impairing violations before the 2022 pilot and after the 2022 pilot for pilot-buildings as compared to eligible buildings, and we found that for rent impairing violations in pilot buildings–
[interposing] For what violations?
Rent impairment violations.
Rent- yes.

There were– there was a reduction in those violations for pilot buildings of around 16, nearly 17 percent, whereas for eligible buildings rent impairing violations increased by 38 percent. So, we do see

some benefit. We can’t establish causation, of course, but we did find them.

But it indicates the program is incentivizing the right kind of behavior which is ultimately what this is about, right, incentivising the kind of behavior we want to see or disincentivizing the behavior we don’t want to see. This may or may not be my last question, but the CONH program currently uses changes in ownership to calculate the building quality index, BQI. How does HPD define owner for the purposes of the BQI and how does HPD track when ownership has changed? Because we are interested in application of the CONH to buildings– building owner’s entire portfolio, not just the specific property.

Yeah, thank you for that question. Have noted that proposed change and understand the thinking behind it. I think we would just say that the– there’s limited methodologies for identifying ownership and linking ownership, and so our data will there only be as good as the property registration is. That’s what we use to identify the owner right now.

Which we are going to make an online process after I get that bill back and we change the multiple dwelling registration. Okay, understood.
